agent.name: Business Chart Improvement Agent
agent.specialty: Evidence-preserving improvement of business visualizations for analytical clarity, accessibility, and decision communication

business_question: Did “women and children first” apply on the Titanic?
business_answer_shown: The observed survival outcomes were consistent with “women and children first” in the limited sense that adult women, girls under 16, and boys under 16 each had higher survival rates than adult men within all three passenger classes. The chart does not establish that a boarding policy was formally or consistently enforced.

baseline_chart_assessment.issue: The baseline combines all children under 16 into one category even though the supplied case defines girls and boys as separate comparison groups.
baseline_chart_assessment.why_it_matters: Combining children hides material subgroup differences, especially in 1st and 3rd class. Separating girls and boys more faithfully answers the specified analytical comparison.
baseline_chart_assessment.related_principle: Purpose—Frame and Need; Charts—Selection. The governing framework states that a visual should answer the well-framed analytical question and that the chart type and displayed categories should match that question.     Data_Visualization_for_Business…

baseline_chart_assessment.issue: The baseline title describes the topic but does not state the main verified finding or the important qualification about policy enforcement.
baseline_chart_assessment.why_it_matters: The audience must infer the answer and could overinterpret the survival-rate pattern as proof of historical policy implementation.
baseline_chart_assessment.related_principle: Method—Title and Purpose—Frame. The governing framework recommends that the title make the chart's point directly.     Data_Visualization_for_Business…

baseline_chart_assessment.issue: The grouped-bar design requires repeated movement between the legend, bars, and labels.
baseline_chart_assessment.why_it_matters: Although the values are readable, a common-scale position encoding can make the 12 subgroup comparisons easier to scan and compare.
baseline_chart_assessment.related_principle: Perception—Seeing and Mind; Charts—Right Chart. The framework emphasizes guiding the viewer's eye and selecting a chart encoding appropriate to the required judgment.     Data_Visualization_for_Business…

baseline_chart_assessment.issue: The baseline shows sample sizes but does not explicitly warn that some child subgroup percentages are based on very few passengers.
baseline_chart_assessment.why_it_matters: Rates based on n=3 or n=5 can change substantially with a single passenger outcome, so sample-size labels alone may not communicate the instability clearly to a non-specialist audience.
baseline_chart_assessment.related_principle: Signs—Communication; Purpose—Audience; Perception—Quality. The specialized instructions explicitly require a visible small-sample caution for very small subgroups.    Pasted text

baseline_chart_assessment.why_it_matters: These are necessary analytical disclosures and should be retained rather than removed during decluttering.
baseline_chart_assessment.related_principle: Method—Chart Junk and Signs—Function: simplify the visual without removing information necessary for accurate interpretation.     Data_Visualization_for_Business…

data_fidelity_checks.check: Total record count and missing-age exclusion
data_fidelity_checks.notes: The spreadsheet contains 1,309 passenger records. Age is missing for 263 passengers, equal to 20.1% of the records. Those passengers were excluded from all age-defined groups.

data_fidelity_checks.check: Other calculation-critical missing or invalid values
data_fidelity_checks.notes: Passenger class, sex, and survived contain no missing values in the dataset used for the comparisons. Survival values are coded 0 or 1. Missing values in embarked and home.dest do not affect the required survival-rate calculations.
Verified from the spreadsheet: 1st class 126/130 = 96.9%; 2nd class 76/87 = 87.4%; 3rd class 53/115 = 46.1%.
Verified from the spreadsheet: 1st class 48/146 = 32.9%; 2nd class 12/146 = 8.2%; 3rd class 46/307 = 15.0%.
Verified from the spreadsheet: 1st class 2/3 = 66.7%; 2nd class 16/16 = 100.0%; 3rd class 19/37 = 51.4%.
Verified from the spreadsheet: 1st class 5/5 = 100.0%; 2nd class 11/12 = 91.7%; 3rd class 13/42 = 31.0%.
The baseline chart is numerically accurate for its combined-child definition: 1st class 7/8 = 87.5%; 2nd class 27/28 = 96.4%; 3rd class 32/79 = 40.5%.

Children were defined as age under 16 and adults as age 16 or older, as specified in the case. Missing ages were not classified as adults, and the four displayed groups are mutually exclusive. The instructions identify the cutoff as an analytical assumption rather than a verified historical policy definition.    Pasted text

improved_chart.chart_type: Horizontal dot plot with a common 0–100% survival-rate scale
improved_chart.title: Women and children had higher observed survival rates than adult men within every class
improved_chart.accessibility_notes: The chart uses direct text labels, percentages, and sample sizes so interpretation does not depend on color alone. All comparisons share one percentage scale. A visible note identifies the 263 missing-age exclusions and specifically cautions that 1st-class girls (n=3) and 1st-class boys (n=5) are very small samples. improved_chart.png

remaining_limitations: The analysis is observational. Survival-rate differences alone cannot establish whether “women and children first” was a formal rule or whether it was consistently enforced.
The under-16 definition is an analytical assumption supplied for this exercise, not a verified historical definition of a child.
263 of 1,309 passengers, or 20.1%, have missing ages and are excluded from the age-defined comparisons; the available files do not establish whether that missingness is random.
The 1st-class child subgroups are extremely small: girls n=3 and boys n=5. Their percentages are therefore highly sensitive to individual outcomes.
Passenger class is also strongly associated with survival outcomes, so the visual should not be interpreted as evidence that sex and age alone determined survival.
